text: IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE G

Gn June 2, 2026, the City Council unanimously voted to place Measure G on the NovembGSÄ26, general municipal election ballot. If approved by a majority of San Carlos voters, Measure G would authorize a one-half cent general retail transactions and use (sales) tax within the City ofsah Carlos ("Proposed Tax"). A on'lalf cent rate equates to an extra $0.50 per $100 purchased. The City estimates that the Proposed Tax will provide an additional $6,000,000 in annual revenue. Revenues raised from the Proposed Tax would go into the City's general fund to pay for any lawful City program, improvement, or service including those identified in the ballot question. The Proposed Tax would be imposed starting on April 1 , 2027 and remain in effect for fourteen (14) years until Mard'aG41 unless extended by a majority of SGÖarlos voters voting at a subsequent election. The Proposed Tax would be paid in addition to the existing 9.375% sales tax, for a total sales tax rate of 9.875% in the City6f San Carlos. The Proposed Tax would be collected at the same time and in the same manner as existing sales taxes and there would be no change to exemptions such as groceries, prescription medications and diapers. Unlike the existing sales tax, all revénues raised by the Proposed Tax would remain in the City and woÜld not be•shared with the State, County or-any other agency. By placing Measure G on the ballot, the City complies with California Revenue and Taxation Code section 7285.9 and Article XIII C of the California Constitution (Proposition 21 8), both of which require the Proposed Tax to be approved by a majority of the voters voting in the election. A "yes" vote on Mea6öG is a vote in favor of the Proposed Tax. A "no" vote on Meas6V8E is a vote against the- Proposed Tax. The above statement ié an impartial analysis ofrMeasure G. text: %raft-BallotArgument in Favor of Measure
Vote YES on Measure for a safe, strong San Carlos

San Carlos is known as the City of Good Living because generations of residents have invested in our safe streets, clean parks, reliable local services, and unmatched quality of life. But those basics do not maintain themselves and San Carlos faces sharp increases in costs to fund public safety, maintain streets and parks, and provide quality services to residents.

This half cent sales tax provides locally controlled funding to fix potholes, repair aging streets and sidewalks, improve storm drains, maintain parks and community facilities, support emergency response, and keep San Carlos neighborhoods safe and well cared for.

Families and local businesses are already facing higher costs, and voters will be asked to consider several measures on November's ballot. That is exactly why Measure deserves careful consideration. It provides local money for local needs. The funds generated will stay in San Carlos, cannot be taken by the State or County, and are subject to independent audits and public disclosure.

Putting off basic maintenance does not save money. Cracked sidewalks, failing sewers, aging park amenities and infrastructure continue to require our attention. This Measure will ensure San Carlos address everyday problems before they become bigger and even more costly.

Endorsed by local leaders, Labor, Fire, San Carlos business owners, and public safety professionals, Measure is not about expanding government. It's about investing in the quality of life we enjoy, the streets we drive, the sidewalks we travel with our kids, the parks where families gather, and the emergency services we count on when minutes matter.
Join us in supporting this sensible, locally-controlled solution to maintaining a safe, strong San Carlos for enerations to come. www.YesforSanCarlos.com.

text: Rebuttal to Argument in Favor of Measure G CITY OF SAN CARLOS CITY CLERK'S DEPARTMEI [start of argument]
Reject this meritless sales tax hike!

Proponents' argument is authored by a professional municipal PR consultant and cosigned by a slate of City Hall insiders masquerading as ordinary "residents." But notice: they don't mention one budget figure. They won't talk numbers, because they can't defend them.
As an independent San Carlos resident, I audited City Hall's figures so you don't have to.
As detailed in our "argument against," City Hall wants to tax us up to 12 times its estimated budget deficit, totaling $84M!
Behind their usual theater over "public safety" and "emergency services," City Hall wants a blank-check general tax to fund $200M in capital projects (as stated in their June mailer).
They want to bypass the 213 supermajority requirement for a special tax (or bond) because they know they lack voter buy-in. Worse, this deficit stems from councilmembers' bad choices:

They paid consultants $200,000 to market this tax to us. e They are spending $7M for Harrington Park "upgrades" — replacing natural kids' play spaces with concrete, and only backing down from a $1 M water fountain after public outcry. • They want to fund an absurdly overpriced $112M bicycle crossing over Highway 101.
Don't be fooled by their spin on "iocal control" — true local control means keeping $6M/year in our community to protect local businesses, not funding councilmembers' pet projects.
Otherwise, San Carlos families will be stuck paying for their extravagance on every online order, delivery, and vehicle purchase — for 14 years!
Force City Hall to change its spending priorities. Vote NO!
[end of argument]

text: Rebuttal to Argument Against Measure CITY OF SAN CARLOS CITY CLERK'S DEPARTMENT
The argument against Measure misses the point.
Measure is not about regional politics, expanding government, or an anti-tax talking point. Measure is about investing in San Carlos.

That's why Measure is supported by San Carlos residents who are former public safety officials, parks and recreation leaders, youth sports leaders, small business owners, parents and seniors, who know this community and rely on its services every day.

San Carlos residents understand that safe streets, sidewalks, storm drains, parks, community facilities, and emergency response do not maintain themselves. Potholes don't get smaller with time. Cracked sidewalks don't become safer by waiting. Aging storm drains and public facilities don't become cheaper to fix later.
No one likes paying more. But Measure is a modest, locally controlled way to invest in the basics that San Carlos residents rely on.

The No argument calls Measure a "blank check." That's false. Measure includes independent audits, public disclosure, and local control. Funds stay in San Carlos and can't be taken by the State or the County.

Voters will see several tax measures on the ballot. Look carefully at each. Measure is the one focused on San Carlos streets, San Carlos parks, San Carlos sidewalks, San Carlos storm drains, San Carlos community facilities, and San Carlos emergency response.
Vote with the San Carlos families, small businesses, seniors, parks and youth sports leaders, and former public safety leaders who are invested in San Carlos.
